#936. Russia is back in world sport, but who is drug testing its athletes?

DW has found that three-quarters of Russia's weightlifting team had no independent out-of-competition testing before this year's world championships, despite the country's doping history.

Fresh questions have emerged over Russia's return to world sport after figures reviewed by DW showed that only four of the 16 Russian weightlifters competing at this year's world championships underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing Agency (ITA).

Two-time European champion Anastasiia Romanova, who previously served a two-year doping ban, was among those not tested by the ITA during the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly anti-doping reports.

By comparison, all 13 members of the North Korean team underwent at least one ITA test during the same period. North Korea, like Russia, has a history of doping violations in weightlifting.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The ITA, which runs weightlifting's anti-doping program, told DW that it tested all 16 Russian weightlifters "ahead of their participation in the event." DW understands those tests were conducted in Ningbo, China, where the championships are being held.

In a power sport like weightlifting, performance-enhancing drugs are most beneficial during training, when athletes build strength and muscle mass in the months before competition. Some drugs, such as anabolic steroids, may be harder to detect by the time the competition comes around.

Rob Koehler, head of the athlete-led movement Global Athlete, called the lack of out-of-competition testing "absurd."

"Out-of-competition testing is the backbone of anti-doping," Koehler told DW. "Everybody knows there's going to be testing at the event. But not everybody knows when they're going to be tested 365 days a year outside events. It's concerning that the ITA doesn't see this as a red flag."

Marta Nawrocka, the ITA's spokesperson, said that Russian athletes were among the 10 most-tested nationalities in weightlifting this year. She also defended the fact that only two Russian weightlifters feature in the sport's highest-priority testing pool, saying inclusion is based on performance and risk profiles.

"Russia's history of doping in weightlifting remains an important factor in the ITA's risk assessment and testing priorities," Nawrocka said. "Russian weightlifters remain subject to substantial testing activity."

"You simply can't treat Russia like any other country," he said. "It has to have more scrutiny. It has to have more testing. If you don't do that, you're undermining athlete confidence in the system."

The International Weightlifting Federation did not respond to a request for comment.

Weightlifting was one of the sports most implicated in Russia's state-sponsored doping scandal, which came to light after the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics. It ranked second only to athletics for the number of positive cases identified by Canadian lawyer Richard McLaren in his 2016 report commissioned by WADA, the global anti-doping watchdog.

The scandal led to dozens of Russian athletes being banned across numerous sports. RUSADA, Russia's anti-doping agency, has remained suspended for most of the past decade.

As a result, its Moscow laboratory cannot analyze urine and blood samples, meaning samples collected by the agency must be sent abroad for analysis under what WADA described as a "strict chain of custody."

WADA said it continued to monitor RUSADA but had been unable to gain access to the country to review the agency's suspension because of the "ongoing geopolitical situation."

It added that RUSADA had "collected thousands of samples … including hundreds from weightlifters" so far this year.

"Given the history, WADA remains vigilant when it comes to Russia," James Fitzgerald, WADA's spokesperson, told DW. "We must ensure that no stone is left unturned when it comes to verifying that all the proper testing and other anti-doping activities are taking place."

Despite being suspended, RUSADA still has the power to investigate and prosecute anti-doping cases involving Russian athletes, which critics find difficult to reconcile.

"It's a compounding problem that WADA is still giving them a free pass when it can't even get into Russia to see what they're doing," said Koehler, WADA's former deputy director general.

"There's simply no oversight and no accountability. And quite frankly, I don't think there ever really has been."

Critics also argue that ongoing questions over RUSADA's leadership and independence suggest that little has been fixed in the decade since the McLaren report.

Even the International Olympic Committee (IOC), whose president, Kirsty Coventry, supports the full return of Russian athletes, has acknowledged a "lack of confidence" over RUSADA's governance.

Nawrocka said the IOC had "recently entrusted" the ITA with an expanded role within Russia in the run-up to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, but did not explain what the role would involve or when it might begin.

In April, investigative outlet The Insider reported that Veronika Loginova, the agency's head, was in a long-term relationship with an alleged FSB officer. The FSB, Russia's domestic security service, played a central role in covering up positive drug tests at the Sochi Games.

Loginova did not respond to questions for this article but dismissed the allegations at the time as "all this nonsense," writing in an email that she believed "sport exists separate from politics."

WADA confirmed to DW only that its investigations unit was examining the allegations against Loginova and that the inquiry was ongoing.

#934. Fan voice on board key to ending Celtic unrest - club legend McStay

Paul McStay is a regular guest at Celtic Park

Celtic legend Paul McStay says having a supporters representative on the board would be a significant step to halting the unrest between the club and the fans.

Issues have arisen around a perceived lack of investment in the Scottish Premiership outfit and underachievement in Europe, with one prominent supporters group recently boycotting matches in protest.

Former Scotland international McStay played his entire club career at Celtic, making more than 500 league appearances between 1981 and 1997 and winning three league titles, four Scottish Cups and a League Cup.

Now he is involved with a collection of season-ticket holders, whose aim is to have more say in how the club is run.

The former captain has made his opinion known to members of the board and believes "healthy debate" can resolve the "disconnect".

Why Celtic's next three games could set AGM tone

"I think there's issues that have to be resolved just now," McStay said. "When Celtic players, management, directors and supporters are all as one, we will be successful or have a great chance of being successful so my hope is that happens again.

"To me, it's healthy debate that's required and come up with a solution that helps our drive forward - domestically maintain the success and in Europe. I think that's what the fans want."

In just under a fortnight, Celtic shareholders will gather at the ground for the club's annual general meeting.

Given the chaos of last year's event, there will be extra eyes and ears on the 2026 AGM on 1 December. And McStay wants change to try and avert more problems.

"The idea is to get enough equity in the club to allow the supporters to have a representative on the board and to me that's important.

"I know the directors and they just want the best for Celtic. We are allowed opinions and I voice my opinions to them, slightly different from what they're thinking.

"To have regular Champions League football is what Celtic supporters are hoping for and I think we can achieve that. But just now I think there's a few things that need to be talked about, debated and hopefully we can move forward as a club."

#933. Janine van Wyk: ‘Our rooms were empty … no mattresses, no lightbulbs and not a drop of water’

In an extract from the former South Africa captain’s book, she details less than ideal Wafcon 2006 preparations

I was just a year into my international career when we qualified for my first Wafcon, which was then called the African Women’s Championship (AWC) and was held in Nigeria in 2006. I was extremely excited but very nervous to participate in this tournament, more so when it was announced that we would be in the same group as the hosts, and would play them last in the group.

As it turned out, it would be the game that decided who finished top of the group. By then we had beaten Algeria 4-0 and Equatorial Guinea 2-0 and had to travel to Delta State to take on the hosts. I’d heard that Nigeria was the toughest country to travel to and I was about to realise why. It’s become common knowledge that South Africans and Nigerians are massive rivals on the football field but also don’t really get on off it.

We felt unwelcome from the moment we arrived and we were not the only team to experience this. Nigeria exploited all avenues to play mind games with their opposition and to make them lose focus on the matches.

We arrived early in the morning at the Murtala Muhammed international airport in Lagos and faced our first test: how to retrieve our luggage. Only one carousel was working, which meant we had to wait a long time for our bags to arrive. We had a training session planned for later in the day and were all eager to get to the hotel, settle in and prepare for our first practice.

As we stepped out the airport doors, we looked for the bus that was to take us there, but we didn’t see one anywhere. As players, we were irritable and impatient, and starting to show it. Some of us were slumped on our bags, others had taken up residence on the pavement, and we were all cranky, especially as it took over an hour before a bus arrived.

Like in Mozambique a few years before, the bus was too small. Another 21-seater and we were 27 – 20 players and seven support staff, as well as all our luggage. Luckily, most of us had experience of how to squeeze in and so we knew the drill. We also had the advantage of our bags travelling in a smaller vehicle behind the bus, so the only challenge was fitting all the bodies in.

Generally, we saw the lighter side of these things and laughed as some of us got comfortable on the floor and others had to make do with a teammate’s lap. But we lost our sense of humour when we realised we had no air-conditioning and the drive was going to last at least another hour. Some grumbling ensued, but we knew better than to complain at such an early stage, and it seemed that things would get better soon.

When we got to the hotel, the building that greeted us looked fairly new from the outside, with freshly painted walls and a manicured garden at the entrance. But when we walked through the doors, it looked as though the hotel was in the process of being renovated, and the outside was clearly the bit that had been made up first. It still looked like a decent place, so we weren’t too worried, and the smell of new paint and the sight of workers installing lights made us feel special as the first group of people staying in this hotel.

All of us were looking forward to being in our rooms and the chance to shower and relax before training. It was only when I saw maintenance workers carrying still-sealed mattresses to the rooms that it occurred to me that we were being put up in a hotel that was not fully ready for guests. I was only half-right. Actually, it was not ready at all.

When we got to our rooms, they were empty: no mattresses on the beds, no lightbulbs in the lamps and, worst of all, not a drop of water in the taps. This made us all a little worried, but we were told it would be sorted out as soon as we had finished our training. We did have lunch at the hotel, although by now I was suspicious of things and particularly of the spread of fish and chicken, and then left for training. At least that went smoothly, and we expected to get back to suitable accommodation. No such luck.

We returned to beds being made but still had no lights or running water. After a training session in extremely warm conditions, we were all dripping with sweat from head to toe and we had to make another plan. A few of our players spotted a river just outside the hotel and said they were going to go there to rinse themselves off. I thought they were joking.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

When I looked again, the players had stripped down to their tights and sports bras, wrapped themselves in their pristine white hotel towels with their toiletries in hand and were heading out the door. If I wanted to be clean, I realised, I had to join them. My hesitation was twofold: I had never washed in a river before and wasn’t sure whether it was hygienic, but I was also still quite young and didn’t want to expose my body in public. I had to get over my qualms quite quickly. Fortunately, we didn’t have to wash in the river again. No one knows how, but when we opened the taps the following day, the water gushed out.

With that kind of preparation, and Nigeria being as strong a team as they were, it was hardly a surprise that we lost 2-0. We experienced Nigeria’s off the field tactics first-hand. I did have one happy memory from the match, though. The Nigerian centre-back, Onome Ebi, who would go on to become the first African to play in six World Cups between 2003 and 2023, gave me her jersey. We both wore No 5 and she was the first international to give me her shirt. Given how much my Banyana Banyana jersey meant to me, I understood how special and symbolic this moment was, and I have stored it in my memory to this day.

This is an edited extract from 185: The Janine van Wyk Story is published by Karavan Press and available on Amazon in the United Kingdom.

#932. Chelsea snatch late winner vs PSG to move top of WCL table

Chelsea Women vs Paris Saint-Germain Women. Women's Champions League.

Match report as Chelsea snatched a late 1-0 win against Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League; Veerle Buurman bundled her effort home from close range in the 88th minute; Chelsea now move to the top of the Champions League table with one league phase game to play

Veerle Buurman's late winner snatched a late 1-0 win for Chelsea against Paris Saint-Germain to move them to the top of the Champions League table.

Sonia Bompastor's side looked as if they were heading to back-to-back goalless draws, following the 0-0 draw with BK Hacken last time out in Europe, until Buurman was able to bundle her effort home at the near post in the 88th minute.

The hosts had been the dominant side throughout but were thwarted by Katarzyna Kiedrzynek on more than one occasion.

Alyssa Thompson had come close to breaking the deadlock just before the break after seeing her initial shot and follow-up effort smothered by Kiedrzynek.

The corner for Buurman's timely winner arrived after the PSG goalkeeper got down well to her right to keep Sjoeke Nusken's header out.

Lucy Bronze's delivery and a slight touch on the way through sparked panic among the PSG defence and it was Buurman who reacted first to sweep home the winner, sending her side to the top of the table with one league phase game to go.

The Blues remain unbeaten in Europe, winning three of their five games so far, and are well placed to qualify for the last 16 through the top four automatic qualification spots. They face OH Leuven in their final game, where they will go into it as strong favourites.

Chelsea boss Sonia Bompastor speaking to UEFA:

"I like the resilience from my team. Believing until the end of the game we could score that important goal and it was really important for us to win tonight.

"What I like in my team and squad is the fact they are really flexible; they are really open-minded to changing systems sometimes, adapting to what is happening on the pitch.

"They understand really quickly. I think it was good for us to be able to change, to go to a back four. We wanted to have the width to destabilise them more than we did in the first half."

On her side potentially finishing in the top four: "We knew we had two games left and getting two wins will help us to probably secure top four.

"So we still have things under control and that was why it was really important for us to win."

Chelsea defender Veerle Buurman speaking to Disney:

"It was really important we scored the goal. Winning and three points was really important, especially after the last Champions League game where we drew against Hacken.

"A good team performance. We tried really hard and that I can score a goal is really important for the team."

Chelsea midfielder Keira Walsh speaking to UEFA:

"We spoke about it before the game about wanting to finish the evening on top. We are in a good spot going into the last game.

"It was a massive win. It was tough for us tonight. They defended really well and they're aggressive.

"It was a difficult game physically but to get the win was really important. Hopefully it will push us into the top four."

#931. Pressley calls for national centre to enhance Scottish game

Scotland's men train at Lesser Hampden, while the women and age group squads use Oriam

Scotland would benefit from the creation of a national football centre, argues Dundee head coach Steven Pressley, who likens the current structure of the game to building on sand.

The health of Scottish football is under the spotlight once more following a poor Nations League campaign under new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli, continued club struggles in Europe and concern over the lack of game time for homegrown talent in the Premiership.

"We have to look at it as more of our game as a whole," said Pressley, who was capped 32 times for Scotland.

"There is a lot of talk about how we get our young players playing and more minutes and there are so many opinions around this.

"I want to get behind something. We don't have our own national football facility.

"I went to Hungary with Dundee in the summer and we stayed at their national centre, it was an outstanding facility with terrific pitches, classrooms, seminar rooms, areas for everybody to progress, areas for everybody to connect.

"When I look at our own country just now I think how do we improve all of our coaches, how do we improve all our young players, how do we improve our analysis, how do we improve our sports science, how do we improve our leadership when we don't even have a facility that we can all come together and really move the country forwards?

"Just now I see us trying to build our country on sand and I mean that, we need a foundation where we can finally grow from. Something that we are proud of."

'I see us trying to build our country on sand'

In England, there is St George's Park - a Â£105m national football centre of excellence, which opened in 2012.

The Scottish FA instead uses facilities at the Oriam Sports Performance Centre in Edinburgh and at Lesser Hampden.

They also sporadically use the Sportscotland National Sports Training centre in Largs, as well as facilities at Ravenscraig and Toryglen.

"For us as a country, a top-50 ranked country, not to have that type of facility worries me," added Pressley, who captained Hearts and played for Rangers, Celtic and Dundee United.

"It says a lot about our strategy, our longevity and our long-term vision and we are finally seeing the effects of that. We have shown none of that over the period and it is all horribly catching up with us.

"We need to start with the absolute basics of a facility that we can start to go from, a lot of the other things will come with time but we always want to fix the here and now rather than saying 'OK we need to build something special'.

"As a result of that, we would see great improvements in so many different areas.

"We would see coaches coming together sharing ideas. When I have done things like my university course and my diploma in football management, I did them at St George's Park.

"We all came together there, we all improved our education there. We need to do that in our own country, make our country proud again and really help each other."

#930. 'I persuaded my club to give me a job as a content creator'

If someone would've said to me I'd be doing this as a job when I was 12, I wouldn't have believed them.

My name's Jacob. I'm a content creator, and I work with Bolton Wanderers.

My role here at Bolton is coming up with new ideas for social media, to try new concepts, filming stuff, and then posting them onto Bolton's pages and trying to help people follow the club. In my opinion, I think it's one of the funnest jobs in football, and it's brilliant.

Right. Welcome to Bolton, Larra. I hope I said that right. I'm going to teach you some Bolton twang to help you settle in.

My passion for football when I was growing up started at a very young age. My dad used to take me to the football matches, and I got my very first season ticket when I was five years old in the 2010/11 season, when Bolton was in the Premiership. Being something I loved as a kid, to turn it into my job is amazing.

I work here at least two days a week, obviously filming content, producing content,and then on match day, I'll be filming mostly with fans, and I love it.

As a town? Well, for us, it's lovely. Yeah.

Mondays, meetings. We have the marketing meeting, so that gives you an idea of what the week holds, what I'm going to do on a match day with the fans. And then in the week, I either film in with players, retail, commercial,whatever department needs help producing videos.

Some of the skills I use, I think one of them's got to be communication. You've got to be able to talk to people, talk to fans, and if you're watching this and you're a bit shy, or you think you can't communicate with people as well, I was like that inhigh school, so you learn it as you get older. But working in football, you've got to be adaptable because one minute you're doing a new signing, next minute you're working with the players, next minute it's a match day, next minute the season's over.

I'd say another one is being creative. That's probably the most important one because without being creative, you won't be able to put a video together.

So when I was 16 in high school, that's where my journey started. I did videos, which got me a number of followers. I always struggled in the classroom side in high school, but creating content and creating ideas and being creative, I was always really, really good at in high school, whether that would be doing something drama-related or English, writing, creating stories. I always knew I had a passion for creative pieces of work and being able to now do it as a job, it suits me down to the ground.

I didn't go to college. I didn't go to uni. I left high school with no GCSEs, but I've always had a real passion for football, so that's how I got in contact with Bolton Wanderers. I started doing some videos here at Bolton with the fans and that, and then it turned into going to the training ground and filming with the players, working with the commercial team, retail team, all the different departmentsaround the football club to eventually getting a paid role in football.

I think don't wait for an opportunity to come to you. Get out there and try. If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role there. But if it doesn't, then you've also created a portfolio working with different people, different businesses, different companies, and it's really good for your CV and for future opportunities with different companies.

The highlight of my career so far, probably looking back, being resilient enough to create my own career path in doing something I love.

When you score this season, you might be chuffed.

If you're passionate about football, you're a bit creative, and you're good in front of the camera, content creation infootball might be a job for you.

To find out what other careers you can have in football, explore the BBC Bitesize Follow Your Passion collection.

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, coming up with new ideas for social media, filming videos and posting them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities."

Jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

#929. Hamilton denies lack of trust with Ferrari after strategy issues

Lewis Hamilton ignored instructions from his Ferrari team to pit at recent races in Singapore and Brazil; the Brit insists there is no trust issue; watch the Las Vegas GP weekend on Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 4am on Saturday and the race at 4am on Sunday

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Lewis Hamilton has insisted there is no lack of trust between himself and his Ferrari team despite having overridden orders from the pit wall twice in recent races.

At the Singapore Grand Prix in October and the Sao Paulo Grand Prix earlier this month, Hamilton ignored instructions to pit, with his decision costing him places on both occasions.

The incidents followed several moments earlier in the season where Hamilton had been left frustrated by strategic decisions from Ferrari that failed to optimise his chances.

Asked ahead of this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix whether taking matters into his own hands was indicative of a lack of trust, Hamilton insisted he was pleased with the work of his race engineer Carlo Santi.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The seven-time world champion said: "No, it's definitely not trusting. I think it's just we're constantly working on our communication. I think that it's been a lot better this year.

"Carlo has done an amazing job, and I think there's been a couple of times where it's just those particular two times was not, particularly the last time, was just I didn't have the information I needed, and I got the call at the last minute.

"And we'll just continue to work on the processes. We're super united and working, I think in the right direction."

Formula 1 drivers back return of 'very cool' V8 engines in the future ahead of Las Vegas Grand Prix

Mercedes confirm ADUO turbo upgrade ready for Las Vegas GP with Kimi Antonelli set to run new engine part

Rafael Camara: Haas keep Brazilian driver as Oliver Bearman's team-mate for Las Vegas GP following home debut

Las Vegas GP 2026: Dates, schedule, weather, UK start time and how to watch or stream F1 race in United States live on Sky Sports

Toto Wolff says Mercedes could prioritise George Russell over Kimi Antonelli in final races of 2026 F1 season from Las Vegas GP

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Hamilton has also had to handle controversy with his team-mate Charles Leclerc, after a first-lap clash between the pair at the Mexico City Grand Prix resulted in something of a public fall out.

Hamilton was highly critical of Leclerc for aggressively attempting to challenge him for the lead on the first lap, with Red Bull's Max Verstappen taking advantage of the squabble to win a race that Ferrari likely would have claimed a one-two in had their drivers held position.

Both Hamilton and Leclerc said that a conversation in Brazil the week after the incident had resolved the situation, and the Brit on Wednesday reiterated his confidence in their working relationship moving forwards.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I think Charles is a great driver," Hamilton said. "I think, as I said, the detail we went into about stuff like that in terms of when we close the visor, it's very clear we understand each other.

"We understand each other's boundaries and the ultimate goal, which is to get the best result for the team.

"So, I don't feel that that will be a problem moving forwards, and I have no concerns or worries about racing him. I don't think he does with me either."

Hamilton admitted he is unsure whether Ferrari will be able to challenge for victory in Las Vegas given the circuit is unlikely to suit their car.

The circuit's long straight could expose Ferrari's power unit weaknesses, while the cold temperatures could lead to issues heating up their tyres sufficiently.

Hamilton said: "We've had a car that's been quick through corners. Obviously, yeah, you have the long straight here. I don't know how that's going to be for us.

"We'll do the best job we can, but hopefully we can make up some of the time maybe in some of the corners. We'll have to wait and see."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Regardless of how competitive Ferrari are, Hamilton says the team will use this weekend, and the upcoming final two races of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, to attempt to optimise their plans for the start of the 2027 season.

"This is a period of time… we don't have any new components to test, but this is definitely a really important data point for us to understand and make some changes setup wise, and try some things that we can potentially try to see if everything's working, if there's different elements of the car that we can remove or add, thinking about next year," he said.

"There's some big changes for next year. But otherwise, right now we have to focus on maintain second in the constructors' championship."

#928. Max Dowman shines in England colours and sends another record tumbling

Midfielder’s under-21s winner eclipsed Jude Bellingham’s mark and there was other talent to admire against France

There may have been an Mbappé on the pitch – Ethan, the younger brother of Kylian, with whom he shares a near-identical gait – but by the end there was only one precocious talent on the lips of those watching England overcome France in their under-21s clash. Max Dowman had done it again, lighting up another game, this time in filthy conditions at Ashton Gate. It was fitting he had the final say in a 3-2 win. The noise that accompanied his match-winning goal? Well, beyond the palpable excitement in the stands in Bristol, that would be the sound of the teenager sending yet another record tumbling.

Which one takes your fancy? Take your pick. At 14, playing for Arsenal Under-19s, he became the Uefa Youth League’s youngest goalscorer. This time last year, after taking to the field at Slavia Prague aged 15 and 308 days, Dowman became the youngest player to feature in the Champions League. In March, six months on from his professional debut, he became the Premier League’s youngest goalscorer. He is the youngest player to earn a Premier League winner’s medal. Last month he was presented with three Guinness World Records.

In scoring his first under-21s goal, in the penultimate minute of regular time, Dowman eclipsed Jude Bellingham to become the team’s youngest scorer at 16 years and 320 days, three days after surpassing the Real Madrid midfielder’s record as the under-21s’ youngest player. Bellingham was almost four months older than Dowman when he scored his first goal for the age group, in September 2020. Bellingham made only four appearances for the under-21s, a result of being fast-tracked into the senior team, and Dowman could emulate him again, though he is expected to feature in next summer’s Under-21 European Championship in Albania and Serbia.

The common view from coaches and teammates, and something stressed by Lee Carsley, the under-21s head coach, is that it is easy to forget Dowman is six weeks shy of his 17th birthday. Against France, it was also extremely easy to overlook that this was Dowman’s first start for the under-21s, after a substitute appearance against Portugal last Friday. His first action set the tone on Monday, using his body to box off the ball then jinking up the right flank, zipping it through the legs of Dayann Methalie before skating forward and sending the Sunderland left-back juddering on to his backside.

Dowman exhibited plenty of neat touches, and a couple of effortless first-time passes, but those who have watched him develop say his work rate and willingness to do the other side of the game are among his biggest strengths.

“We look at Max and see how good he is on the ball, how attacking he is, but I thought he was outstanding off the ball,” Carsley said, presumably thinking of the moment Dowman scampered deep into his own half to intercept a stray France pass. He was not finished after scoring either. At one point he had five blue shirts haring after him as he stormed into the France half and, seconds later, his quick feet lured the opposition captain, Nathan Zézé, into a foul on the edge of the France penalty area.

Dowman is among the next wave of players pushing to step up to Thomas Tuchel’s squad, perhaps at its forefront. It is a well-trodden path and the current crop need not look too far for inspiration. Elliot Anderson and Jarell Quansah, both of whom started England’s triumph at the last under-21 Euros in Bratislava, began Sunday’s memorable victory for the seniors in Madrid. Jobe Bellingham and Josh King are the latest players to make the transition into Tuchel’s squad and more will follow.

Jack Hinshelwood and Trey Nyoni, of Brighton and Liverpool respectively, impressed at the base of midfield and the 19-year-old Mikey Moore, another to score on his first start for the under-21s, shone down the left flank, opening the scoring. The Everton midfielder Harrison Armstrong entered as a substitute and supplied Dowman’s winner, and Armstrong’s clubmate Tyrique George also showed promise after replacing Moore. Archie Gray captained the under-21s against Portugal but did not feature on Monday, with Carsley revealing he has spoken to the Tottenham midfielder about Scotland wanting him to switch allegiance. “I just said to him: ‘Keep me in the picture, if it’s something that you were thinking of,’” Carsley said. “I think Archie is very connected to our pathway.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

England’s budding talent is not confined to the under-21s. Carsley took a closer look at Brian Madjo, the imposing 17-year-old striker who scored on his Aston Villa debut in the Super Cup in August, the Manchester United defender Ayden Heaven and the West Brom forward Jimmy-Jay Morgan, who signed from Chelsea in the summer, before his squad departed for Bristol last week, the trio joining the under-21s for four days of training at St George’s Park.

Dowman, after two under-21 appearances comprising a little more than 120 minutes, is putting the squeeze on. “Max is doing something special for his age and he is pushing people a lot older than him,” said Moore, who is on loan from Tottenham at Köln and hopes to face his idol Harry Kane and Bayern Munich on Friday. “He’s a top kid. You kind of forget how old he is. My little brother is 17 and he [Dowman] feels older to me than my little brother … He has been top and everywhere he goes, he just takes that next step.”

#927. How to become a football referee

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and said sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your plan and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

If you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees new referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared."

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful."

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

#926. European shares join a global sell-off as AI spending fears rattle Wall Street and Asian markets

European shares have fallen after sharp losses in Asia and on Wall Street. Doubts over huge AI investments and fears of curbs following the Democrats' US midterm victory have rattled global markets.

European shares fell sharply in early trading on Friday as a global sell-off fueled by concerns over artificial intelligence stocks spread from Wall Street to Asia and Europe.

Fears of curbs on AI data-center spending have added to investors' concerns after Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress.

The pan-European STOXX 600 index dropped 1.6% in early trading, wiping out its gains for the week. Most major European markets fell more than 1%, with media, healthcare and retail stocks leading the declines.

European markets had previously weathered the week's turbulence better than their Asian and US counterparts because of their more limited exposure to AI stocks.

Earlier, Japanese and South Korean shares tumbled after a massive selloff in tech stocks on Wall Street the previous day.

Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei 225 index fell 5.5% in early trade, while Seoul's tech-heavy Kospi index slid as much as 8.8%, triggering a circuit breaker which suspended trading for 20 minutes. Taiwan's benchmark TAIEX index was also down more than 8%.

Asian tech giants including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) have borne the brunt of the artificial intelligence-related selloff.

Samsung plunged nearly 10% while SK Hynix slid over 11%.

Chip-related shares in Japan also took a beating, with Tokyo Electron stock trading down around 9% and Kioxia shedding 13%.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US markets were hammered on Thursday by a sharp retreat in tech stocks, particularly those involved in the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure like data centers.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5.52% and shed as much as $2.5 trillion (roughly €2.23 trillion) in market value, while the broader S&P 500 index plunged 4.4%.

The rout occurred as investors grow increasingly anxious about the colossal AI spending plans and whether they will eventually produce commensurate profits.

The results of the US midterm elections, which saw Democrats seize control of both houses of US Congress, added to the concerns.

A number of Democratic governors-elect campaigned on slowing artificial intelligence development and promised to stop or pause the construction of data centers amid growing public opposition to such projects.

"It's pretty clear there's been a real shift ​in sentiment," Michael McCarthy, chief executive for Australia and New Zealand at online brokerage Moomoo, told the Reuters news agency.

"Market turning points are often accompanied by strong disagreement, and that shows up in the market ​by huge swings in either direction," he said. "That's what we appear to have had — and last night's emphatic sell-down suggests that is the direction that we're now headed in."

#925. Pocognoli’s aspiration for how Scotland must play is in danger of becoming unworkable

The 4-0 debacle against Switzerland has added to the tactical concerns about the head coach’s suitability, just six games into the job

The Scottish Football Association can only cling to a lesson from the past when assessing a worrying international window. Steve Clarke was beleaguered during his early games in charge. Successive 4-0 defeats by Belgium and Russia in 2019 left Clarke with the sense he should have stayed in club management. A revival meant Clarke led his country to three out of four tournaments.

There are, however, fundamental differences between the story of Clarke and that being delivered by Sébastien Pocognoli. Clarke was a pragmatist, whose decades in coaching suggested he had the wherewithal to revive Scotland. Pocognoli, six games into his tenure, is in danger of lurching into the territory of dreamy ideologue whose aspiration for how Scotland must play is unworkable. The meek nature of Scotland’s collapse in the 4-0 loss to a second-string Switzerland was lamentable. The Belgian’s assessment, with overpraise a key theme, raised eyebrows.

Pocognoli’s team scored five goals in six Nations League games, four coming against North Macedonia. They drew blanks in three fixtures. The concession of 10 depicts a team soft against set pieces and in open play. Scotland have wingers who are not appropriately deployed because of dedication to a system. They have an obvious shortage of centre-backs yet Pocognoli picks three at a time. The midfield lacks balance. Not one player under Pocognoli’s watch is consistently excelling.

Pocognoli is obstinate in respect of his tactics. At club level this can work owing to daily work on a training pitch. Scotland are wedded to a 3-4-2-1 that fits too few of their players. There is no transfer window capacity to change that. Pocognoli’s insistence upon his “philosophy” sets off alarm bells. Although his English is strong, it is far from perfect, which raises questions about communication. Scotland do not look well drilled or clear in approach, which was plain in the unimpressive home win against North Macedonia even before the Switzerland debacle.

Unlike with Clarke, there is no detailed body of work to suggest Pocognoli can adapt or oversee improvement. He achieved great success in Belgium, winning the title at Union Saint-Gilloise, before a brief spell at Monaco. The Scottish FA’s deep faith in this 39-year-old, amid all manner of waffle about metrics and analytics, was on the basis of just over 100 games as a manager. It remains probable that the association erred in not sourcing a coach with dugout experience at a country of similar scale to Scotland. This always had the whiff of trying to be too smart by half.

The best Scotland sides are unapologetically horrible to play against, physical, energetic and direct. Shortcomings in skill are offset by attitude. Pocognoli’s version is the opposite on all fronts, ponderous and timid. The Tartan Army, hardly a ferociously demanding lot, have failed to demonstrate any excitement about Pocognoli.

This counts as no ode to Clarke. After seven years, change was required. It was the turn taken by the Scottish FA in implementing a new strategy that looks increasingly dubious.

Footballers are typically selfish beings. For now it suits the Scotland squad – and is fair – to state Pocognoli requires time and that they are behind him. Not only did the body language amid the unravelling in St Gallen suggest otherwise, those players are likely to adopt a different position if focus turns towards them. Scotland’s contingent is heavy on influential, experienced players.

There is no sense of the Scottish FA dispensing with Pocognoli at this point. Not only would such a move be premature, it would deliver an admission of failure that those running the governing body are never keen on providing. They enjoy the trappings and profile provided by the national team without anything like the adjacent accountability. They are assisted in this context by domestic football obsession within the country. There will be grumblings about Pocognoli for a brief period this week before the theme is placed into cold storage.

Next month’s Uefa 2028 qualifying draw, where Scotland will appear from pot three, carries intrigue and danger for Pocognoli. The assumption that Scotland will feature in the tournament is undermined by performances; England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland are co-hosting and a maximum of two spots are open for any of those nations who do not qualify. Not playing in a competition where games will be staged in Glasgow would count as a humiliation for the Scottish FA.

If Scotland face competitive games rather than friendlies in March, which will be determined after the draw, Pocognoli needs stark improvement. Without it, his paymasters would then have a decision to make while looking to keep Euro 2028 dreams alive. The situation is already that acute.

Pocognoli was not part of the Scotland party that landed in Glasgow from Zurich on Tuesday. His family have remained in Belgium. Alone with his thoughts on his journey home, Pocognoli must have pondered the harshness of his new environment. He has the sternest of challenges to quieten legitimate background noise.

#923. AI must be held accountable — value statements won’t protect human dignity

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Cindy Skach is an emeritus professor of law at King’s College London.

There is a striking gap in debates about artificial intelligence. Policy bodies and frontier AI laboratories are borrowing the vocabulary of legal constitutions to guide model development and oversight. However, these statements currently don’t include the institutional safeguards that would make such value commitments work.

In September, the UK Parliament’s Joint Committee on Human Rights published its report on AI regulation. It uses ‘human rights’ more than 100 times in as many pages, but doesn’t discuss which rights should be protected or how. AI firm Anthropic in San Francisco, California, has written a ‘constitution’ for its model Claude. In it, numerous values are listed as the tool’s priorities, including the preservation of user autonomy. Yet some of these values, such as autonomy and well-being, compete with each other, as Anthropic acknowledges. The document does not provide an independent arbiter to adjudicate the conflict, or monitor violations by the AI system.

AI governance requires more than just a declaration. It requires a system of accountability. Specific institutions should constrain the tools’ influence in accordance with specific fundamental values and hold firms accountable to individuals affected by AI transgressions. Lawyers call this constitutionalism.

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare

As a scholar of constitutional law, I see parallels between the current debate on AI governance and how national constitutions have been crafted, broken, borrowed and fixed.

Countries’ constitutions have distinct underlying priorities affecting their design. These fall roughly into two historical approaches (C. Skach Int. J. Const. Law 7, 175–181; 2009). One takes liberty as its priority: describing what people are free to do and what the state should not do to interfere. The other focuses on human dignity: noting not what individuals may do, but what cannot be done to them, regardless of the circumstances or whether they have consented to it.

Germany’s post-war constitutionalism demonstrates the latter. Its founding document, or basic law, was designed in 1949 to put dignity first and foremost — as both the highest guiding value and a constitutional right, the violation of which is actionable in court. It established an independent federal constitutional court, which citizens can approach directly, that became operational two years later. The choice of this value and the legal institutions to protect it were a response to the atrocities of the Nazi regime, in which people became instruments of state objectives.

Frontier AI companies and policymakers should seriously consider using these features of German constitutionalism. When dignity as a constitutional right is violated — by an AI-generated deepfake or by a chatbot that treats a distressed user as just another interaction — the people affected could petition the court directly, and the perpetrator could be stopped and held accountable.

We need a new ethics for a world of AI agents

#921. Exercise coaching boosts colon cancer survival

Evidence suggests exercise can keep more cancer patients alive. But what does "living longer" actually mean, and who does it apply to?

In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.

The question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care.   In the US, that shift is reaching hospital standards. From January 2027, breast cancer centers must screen patients' physical function and recommend exercise or physical therapy where needed.

Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.

The 2025 trial, called CHALLENGE, was led by the Canadian Cancer Trials Group. It began enrolling patients in 2009 and published its results in 2025.

The trial's 889 participants came from six countries, most from Canada and Australia. All had finished surgery and chemotherapy for stage 2 or 3 colon cancer, which had not spread to distant organs.

Half received only health education materials on exercise and healthy eating. The other half additionally met a physical activity consultant for three years.

In the exercise group, the target was similar to adding 45 to 60 minutes of brisk walking, three to four times a week. The amount and type of activity varied from person to person, said Tormod Skogstad Nilsen, a cancer exercise researcher in Norway. But he said participants achieved lasting increases in their physical activity.

Exercise helped. People in the exercise group were less likely to see their cancer come back, to develop a new cancer or to die. In all, 93 had at least one of these setbacks, compared with 131 in the health education group.

In cancer research, living longer usually means a larger share of people is still alive at a given point. It does not promise anyone a set number of extra years.

Eight years after joining CHALLENGE, about 90 of every 100 people in the exercise group were alive, compared with about 83 of every 100 in the health education group. That is about 7% more people alive in the group who had guided exercise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For people without cancer, the evidence comes from studies that follow people's habits and health over many years. These can show a link, but not prove cause and effect. Active people may also eat better or smoke less.

In another 2025 study, more than 85,000 adults in the United Kingdom wore a wrist tracker for a week. Over about six years, those who moved most had a 26% lower risk of 13 cancers, including breast and colorectal cancer, than those who moved least.

Even light activity, such as household chores, was linked to lower risk. The link held after researchers accounted for lifestyle, weight and other health conditions.

Earlier research, based on people's self-reporting, has led to similar conclusions. A 2016 analysis of 1.44 million adults in the US and Europe linked free-time activity to a lower risk of many cancers, largely regardless of weight or smoking.

A trial to prove prevention is unlikely: Many cancers take years to develop, so it would need huge numbers of people followed for a long time.

CHALLENGE included only people with colon cancer. But how it picked participants offers a clue: Before joining, they had to pass a fitness test.

Anna Campbell, a professor of clinical exercise science at Edinburgh Napier University in Scotland, sees that as a guide.

"I think patients with any other cancer stage II and III who have a reasonable baseline level of fitness and no major comorbidities that would prevent them from undertaking moderate to vigorous activity could be considered for similar interventions," she said. Comorbidities are other health conditions.

Nilsen noted some people decline to join exercise trials because they feel too unwell or tired, or do not want to exercise. "Hence, study populations are typically younger, 'healthier', and most times slightly more motivated compared to a clinical population," he said.

The coaching aimed to make activity a lasting habit, and Campbell said that is where the trial's value lies.

"The main success of the study is that it enabled the participants to become independent exercisers staying active in a safe and effective and individualized way," she said.

Nilsen agreed. Helping people become more active "in their own environment," without depending on a well-equipped training center, "would likely lead to more sustainable activity behavioral changes," he said.

He is wary of fixed targets, however. "Exercise should be tailored to each individual and the challenges they face, rather than striving to reach a given minimum of exercise required," though health care resources may not always allow it, he added.

In a 2024 survey of 549 people with cancer, only one in 10 had been referred to an exercise service. Yet almost three in four thought their oncologist should raise the subject.

"There are some excellent examples of effective pathways but these are few and far between," said Campbell. Good services bring everyone on board, from surgeons to community fitness instructors.

"Ideally, one person in the clinical setting needs to champion the program to link all the team together."

Campbell expects CHALLENGE's regular coaching will be cut back in everyday care. Apps and live online group sessions could still work, she said, if run by properly trained staff.

One recent study of live online exercise engaged patients from poorer backgrounds, in rural areas and with advanced cancer. "It answered some of the barriers, such as cost, travel and lack of confidence," she said.

Patients can ask their care team what exercise is safe for them and what support exists.

According to Nilsen, a training session can bring structure and company. "You made it here, despite your feeling unwell or fatigued this morning, so you feel mastery based on that," he said.

#919. Reliving the drama: England and Argentina stars watch 1986 classic with fresh eyes

A new film about the historic World Cup quarter-final clash finds new angles for a new generation

“Is there anything new to say about it?” Gary Lineker asked the producer Flora Fernandez-Marengo when she first approached him to take part in The Match, a documentary about the 1986 World Cup quarter-final between England and Argentina. Flora told an audience at the London film festival premiere of the film that she played her best card then and showed Lineker an image of Maradona with Queen in 1981, during the band’s tour of Argentina. Maradona wearing a union jack T-shirt and Freddie Mercury an Argentina strip. It worked. Lineker said yes.

The rock’n’roll angle, with Brian May as a talking head, is one of the very few details the film-makers added to Andrés Burgo’s book, The Match, on which the documentary is based. The directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco play with the timeline, hopping between past and present across 91 minutes, the exact duration of the match itself. Anecdotes that now form part of Argentina’s football folklore are spliced with excellent archive material.

“There are two types of humans,” Jorge Valdano narrates, “Carlos Bilardo and everyone else.” Ricardo “El Gringo” Giusti recounts how he buried a sweet in the pitch before kick-off of every game, just one of the many cábalas the Argentina squad religiously followed under pressure from their obsessive manager. On the eve of the match with England, the players requested lighter shirts as the official ones were too heavy when drenched in sweat. Footage of women working at the squad hotel hand-stitching the numbers on to light T-shirts bought locally, shot by the players themselves with a handheld camera, conveys an intimacy in stark contrast to grainy archive material depicting British explorers in the South Atlantic.

Rather than run-of-the-mill talking head-style interviews with members of both teams, the interviewees are shot in monochrome, widescreen closeups, “like Roman statues”, as Cabral told the Guardian. Like monuments to themselves, the camera lingers on their eyes. What are they watching? We don’t know if they see what we see, if they are reliving the match, or seeing a cut of the actual film.

The documentary pivots around Diego Maradona’s two goals. I have long ceased to think of them as two separate goals. They are a single event, a handful of minutes when everything that is possible in football happened before our very eyes: the ugly, rule-breaking handball followed by the spectacular, beautiful gambeta. The film cleverly uses a sequence of stills taken by the Mexican photographer Alejandro Ojeda Carbajal to prove the handball, with a tongue-in-cheek nod to the paradox that they have been credited and licensed through the Englishman Bob Thomas ever since.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Films about football are hard to get right because football is a narrative form in itself. This one comes pretty close to being as good as it gets. Slick and elegant, if at times a little too glossy, The Match is an excellent piece of work filled with beautiful images, such as the crisp vintage radio illustrating soldiers listening to the game in the trenches. There are also newsreels of Margaret Thatcher and Argentinian generals at the height of the Falklands/Malvinas conflict; a score that includes Queen and giants of Argentinian rock such as Charly García. Nostalgia, history, and the backdrop of the war, handled with respect and sensitivity.

The perversity of Argentina’s military is reflected in images of an emaciated soldier spliced to the voice of a general who dismisses claims the troops were cold and starving: “They probably eat better than they did at home.” Lou Armour, a British veteran, explains he couldn’t see young Argentinians as the enemy. “We both suffered a tragedy,” Cabral says. “I’m interested in the human duality in which we go from killing each other to hugging each other.” Cabral asks when a match starts and when it ends, and also when a conflict does so.

Valdano reads Juan López y John Ward, a Jorge Luis Borges poem about the war, in Spanish. Lineker, sitting by his side, utters “very moving”, also in Spanish. English and Spanish coexist throughout the film, including in the scene showing a table football game in which John Barnes and Peter Shilton take on against Giusti, Óscar Ruggeri and Jorge Burruchaga. Burruchaga, the scorer of the winning goal in the 1986 World Cup final, cheers his opponent: “Vamos, Peter!”

An audience containing young people reacted to the documentary with a standing ovation at the London screening, where Shilton was the only cast member present. In Buenos Aires, the release of the documentary, which coincided with this summer’s World Cup, saw cinemas packed with young people. For a generation in England and Argentina who never saw the 1986 classic, almost everything in The Match is new.

The Match is in UK cinemas from 20 November

#918. Were any current Man City players signed during charges period?

Manchester City captain Ruben Dias has made more than 250 club appearances since his arrival in 2020

No member of Manchester City's current squad was signed during the period in which an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

Those offences all came between 2009 and 2018. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed against all of the charges against them.

The club's longest-serving first-team player who was purchased from another club is Portuguese centre-back and club captain Ruben Dias, who joined from Benfica in 2020.

Norway striker Erling Haaland is the next longest-serving arrival, joining from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2022.

Midfielder Phil Foden is the only player to have played for the club during the period in which they breached the league's financial rules, but was not a senior signing having come through the club's youth ranks.

Foden, 26, made his first-team debut in a Champions League match against Feyenoord in November 2017.

Like Foden, versatile midfielder Rico Lewis is also a product of the club's academy but did not make his senior debut until August 2022.

All of the club's other senior players were signed between 2023 and 2026.

#917. ‘The game is in danger’: PFA head Maheta Molango on Fifa, Infantino and football’s future

At a potentially critical juncture for football, the PFA’s chief executive talks about the organisation, wider fears in the game and why the Folarin Balogun affair was ‘scandalous’

After five years in charge of the Professional Footballers’ Association, what has Maheta Molango learned? “The game is in danger,” the 44-year-old says. “I’ve learned that the game I loved and led me to first play and then advise and then lead a club and today to lead the PFA, is in danger because it is being forgotten.”

In 2026, with football ubiquitous on all platforms, with a World Cup that generated $15bn (£11.4bn) in revenue, and with attendances across the English pyramid growing year on year, it may seem hard to imagine forgetting about the game. But Molango’s unique perspective as head of the players’ union for England and Wales observes a different picture; one where the future of the sport is being determined not by what will maintain its popularity, but what will make the most money.

“What I’ve seen over the last few years is that I attend meetings where we talk about everything except for the game,” Molango says. “And I think we’ve allowed people to enter the game that did not enter it for the right reasons. They did not enter the game to make it better. They did not enter the game because they loved it. They entered the game because they saw money in the game and because they saw influence in the game. And I’m very concerned about that because, ultimately, if you don’t have a good game, if you don’t have a good product, you don’t have an industry.”

Molango is speaking at a potentially critical juncture for the future of football. Wednesday is the deadline for candidates for the role of Fifa president to put their name forward for March’s election. Gianni Infantino appears likely to win an unprecedented fourth term despite the cascade of scandal that has dogged much of his decade in charge. Infantino’s tenure has also brought about enormous changes of which Molango, whose union had 345 members playing at this year’s World Cup, 27.6% of the total, is highly critical.

The expansion of the World Cup is one central issue; where 32 teams became 48 at the men’s tournament this past summer and perhaps 64 in 2030. The changes, which players’ unions say were made without consulting players, have led to knock-on effects on the calendar that mean the PFA is pursuing Fifa through the European courts to ensure “the legal rights of players to take guaranteed and protected breaks”. But they have also damaged, in Molango’s mind, what should be the sport’s most precious event – and for spurious reasons.

“Can anyone who really believes in the concept of the World Cup think that having a 64-team tournament makes sense?” he says. “We may as well call it a summer friendly tournament. And I cannot buy the narrative that says: ‘Oh, it’s about making football truly global.’ That’s just not true. It’s disrespectful to think that people in the Congo want to be gifted access to the World Cup. We don’t need favours, we just need opportunities. We want to deserve to be at the World Cup, we don’t need it to be gifted to us, thank you very much. Don’t treat us as if we need to thank you for giving us something.”

Then there is the question of integrity. Summer’s World Cup brought an incident which, for many in the game, crossed a red line: the overturning of the suspension awarded to the USA’s Folarin Balogun, after an intervention by Donald Trump. “What happened with Balogun is scandalous,” Molango says. “Because my son can say to me: ‘Football is corrupt.’ It’s unacceptable that you’ve allowed a situation where people can think that. Governing bodies must protect the integrity of the game and not just that, the perception of integrity as well.”

Molango was born in Switzerland to a Congolese father and an Italian mother. He is an Italian national and began his career as a professional footballer in Spain, at Atlético Madrid. He made no appearances for the club, however, before moving to Brighton (a club that was a different proposition in 2005: “We were playing at the Withdean and I was washing my own kit at home”). From there he moved across and down the English football pyramid before finishing in Spain. After retirement he retrained in Spain as a lawyer , establishing the country’s first sports law practice, before he became the chief executive of Mallorca. He took the club to the depths of the third tier, then back to La Liga in consecutive seasons before taking charge at the PFA, replacing the longtime leader Gordon Taylor at a time of tumult for the organisation.

To visit the PFA’s smart, new offices in London’s Liverpool Street, bedecked in replica kits and with a timeline of players’ developing rights in the entrance hall, is to see an organisation that has come out the other end of an intensive period of reform. An independent review into the PFA’s governance was launched in 2018 after concerns over the use of funds. The outcome led not only to Molango’s appointment but also to the introduction of a players’ board – now led by the impressive Omar Beckles alongside Ben Davies of Tottenham and Chelsea’s Lucy Bronze among others – as well as non-executive directors and a committee focusing on the ethics of the organisation.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“The PFA had a credibility issue,” Molango says. “We called an independent expert. They came in, they assessed, and they changed the governance. So I think we led the way. We demonstrated that sometimes you don’t need to be rotten to be wanting to change, you just need to acknowledge that things move on.”

Ten years after the reforms that followed the Sepp Blatter era, Molango believes that Fifa must change again. “It’s a sick system,” he says. “and for me we shouldn’t be talking about individuals, we should be talking about governance. The system as currently constructed is a system that will always foster the wrong behaviour. Because inevitably the decision taken will not be for what’s good for the game. It will be for what’s good for the next election.”

If change doesn’t occur, there is no guarantee in Molango’s mind that football’s status as the world’s favourite sport, and a cultural unifier, will continue. “We live in a world where there’s tough competition for entertainment and what I think will happen is that people will lose interest and move on,” he says. “They move on to other sports, to other sources of entertainment and in the end we’ll kill the industry. We’ll kill it because we’re no longer the only players in the playground. There’s a lot of people who have a good product. We need to go back to focusing on the quality of our product. Because football has a real problem.”

#916. Who is close to a yellow card suspension in Champions League?

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

Yellow cards that result in a red card during a match do not count towards a player's tally, as a separate suspension will be served.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of the Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk's Marlon Gomes, Villarreal's Santiago Mourino and Inter Milan's Hakan Calhanoglu are each on three yellow cards, putting them on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's earlier clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

*denotes two yellows that resulted in a red card

The following players will miss the next round of league phase matches following either a yellow or red card suspension:

Matheus Cunha (Manchester United - red card suspension)

#915. What to know about the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship

As ice hockey's governing body continues to wrangle over how to respond to a CAS order to reinstate Russia to international play, the top women's tournament gets underway in Denmark without Russia.

Since its inception in 1990, the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship has almost always been held in the spring — apart from 2021 and 2022, when the COVID-19 pandemic saw it moved to the summer. This year, though, the tournament, being hosted by Denmark from November 6 to November 16, is being held in November for the first time.

The idea is make it easier for all of the world's best players to participate. Since its inception in 2023, the North America-based Professional Women's Hockey League (PWHL), widely considered the world's best, has had to pause its season to allow players to take part in the Worlds. This is no longer necessary, as the PWHL's regular season doesn't open until December.

"This gives the women's game a unique selling point," International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) President Franz Reindl recently told the SID news agency. "Because the PWHL season begins after this, we can be certain that the very best players are participating."

Previously, the teams were divided into a stronger group and a weaker group, with the idea being to avoid, as much as possible, lopsided scores. This is because women's hockey is not as balanced as the men's game, with Canada or the United States having won every tournament since its inception.

Under the old system, all five teams in the stronger Group A advanced to the quarterfinals. Under the new format, four of the five teams advance from both groups. This also sees powerhouses the US and Canada in separate groups, meaning the marquee matchup can't occur early in the tournament.

Group A: USA, Czechia, Switzerland, Germany, Austria

Group B: Canada, Finland, Sweden, Japan, Denmark

No. While the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on October 30 — a week before the opening faceoff of the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship — that the IIHF must allow Russia back into its tournaments during the 2026-2027 season, it made no mention of this tournament. Under the CAS ruling though, the IIHF will be required to include Russia at the 2027 tournament in Quebec City.

As noted above, either Canada or the United States has won every edition of this tournament — and indeed the two countries have split Olympic gold medals between them (Canada with five, USA with three) since the sport was introduced to the Winter Games in 1998. There is nothing to suggest that this is about to change in Herning and Esbjerg, although Canada enters the tournament with a vastly different roster from the one that won Olympic silver in Milano in February.

Among those looking to break this North American domination are Finland, the only other team ever to have made it to a world championship final and Switzerland, who took bronze in Milan.

The United States and Canada will play in generic kits provided by the International Ice Hockey Federation's official supplier due to an ongoing commercial rights dispute.

The Canadian federation, Hockey Canada, said in a statement on Wednesday that its players would be wearing jerseys designed by True Hockey instead of their Bauer jerseys featuring the national team logo. USA Hockey has confirmed that its players too will be wearing jerseys without its national emblem.

"While we have yet to see the jersey Canada will be playing in on Friday, our team remains focused on the tournament and representing our country proudly on and off the ice," Hockey Canada said.
